newsitem.title: USA: Albright said planning visit to Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Albright said planning visit to Hong Kong.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was expected to announce on Tuesday that she will visit Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, administration sources said.

Albright was expected to make the announcement in an evening speech to the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland. She met Hong Kong democracy activist Martin Lee on Monday and he urged her to visit the colony for the handover.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters Albright would make "quite significant news" in her speech but he would not say what it was. Other officials told Reuters she would announce the Hong Kong visit.
It was not clear if she would also go to China but that would seem unlikely since she just visited there in February.

"This speech will focus on the major relationships that the United States has in the Asian Pacific region with Japan and Korea, allies of the United States, with China, with many of the Southeast Asian countries that are so important," Burns said. "She'll certainly want to talk about Burma, Hong Kong and a variety of other issues."

The White House was criticised because Vice President Al Gore bypassed Hong Kong on a trip to Asia last month that included a very controversial stop in Beijing. Nevertheless, senior U.S. officials have repeatedly stressed that China's treatment of Hong Kong will be a major factor in the development of Sino-American ties.

Lee, in Washington to stress concerns over an erosion in rights and civil liberties in Hong Kong as China prepares for the takeover, was warmly welcomed by Senate Republicans. The White House then announced that he would also meet Gore this week and President Bill Clinton would drop in on the meeting.
After meeting Albright on Monday, Lee said he had urged her to attend the handover ceremonies. Albright had been mulling a joint invitation from Britain and China.

Speaking to reporters, Lee praised Clinton and Albright for deciding to meet him as evidence that Washington "takes the human rights issues very seriously and is prepared to give recognition to the democratic leadership of Hong Kong."

Lee, a Hong Kong legislator and pro-democracy leader who heads the colony's Democratic Party, reaffirmed support for continued Most Favoured Nation trade status for China and complained that by eroding political and civil freedoms in Hong Kong China was not helping its campaign for MFN renewal.

China on Tuesday accused Lee of trying to incite international forces to meddle in Hong Kong affairs. Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing Lee's U.S. visit and planned meeting with Clinton were part of an attempt to win political capital.

China's choice to be chief executive of Hong Kong after it takes control, Tung Chee-wa, was due to visit Washington next month and would expect to meet Clinton as the British governor, Chris Patten, has in the past. Meeting Lee now will make it easier for Clinton to meet Tung later.
At Tuesday's news briefing, Burns called Lee "one of the most articulate spokespeople for Hong Kong's continued democratic development (and) a very impressive man."

Burns said that in her meeting with Lee Albright "reaffirmed the very strong support that we have always had for the civil liberties of the people of Hong Kong -- that's the rule of law, the protection of the civil liberties of the people and democratic institutions."

Albright also "assured Mr. Lee that Hong Kong was very much on the administration's agenda, that we would continue to speak candidly to senior (Chinese) officials ... about the preservation of Hong Kong's autonomy and way of life after the change of sovereignty, consistent with the Sino-British declaration of 1984," Burns said.

As the transition nears, there is rising concern in the United States as well as in Hong Kong that China is not living up to its promises to permit Hong Kong to function as it has, with considerable civil and political freedoms. U.S. lawmakers increasingly have questioned whether MFN, which grants favourable U.S. trade benefits, should be renewed for China.
